question: The female mind
answer:
Club humor suggested that women not only believed in but even originated many popular superstitions through telling tales to the children in their care. A Club speech observed that for most children, “some superstitious feeling” was “imbibed with his mother's milk.” While the Club reminisced fondly about the "harmless" superstitions of childhood, they asserted that “age and intelligent reason lift the veil of delusion” as the child matured into a man. Any adult who persisted in superstitious belief, by this logic, failed to complete the developmental journey from childhood fantasy to masculine rationality. He remained, embarrassingly, stranded in mental infancy or effeminacy, unsuited to the demands of citizenship. Adult women, by nature of their gender, could never mature into this kind of intellectualism within the logic of the Club, but remained attached to childish beliefs through Club humor. 

Where the Club decried superstitions among the voting public, the state of women's beliefs did not overly concern them at first. Rather, they regarded women as a sort of benevolent lost cause--a demographic unreachable by reason, but nevertheless charming: "The custom pleases her, so why should it not be continued?"

question: Haunted by gender
answer:
Several of the Club's jokes took aim at the spiritualist movement, a movement not incidentally dominated by women whose participants often sympathized with the women’s suffrage movement. 

The Club sarcastically lamented in 1883 that they had “sought in vain for a haunted house, in which to enjoy at least one of our dinners. Evidently ghosts refuse to affiliate with us, though an invitation to meet such on earth will at any future time be eagerly accepted and promptly acted upon.” This offer to dine with a ghost if one could be found mocked those who believed in ghosts, as the Club men made clear that in the absence of 'scientific evidence' they did not believe. While beliefs in "fortune telling and spiritualism" continued "to play upon the weaker side of effete or sickly humanity, there will exist a necessity for just such a bold, brave body of men as compose the Thirteen Club" opined one member. Club men imagined themselves as "bold, brave" through their claims to intellectual reason in contrast to the allegedly compromised intelligence of other demographics.
